Name: mlp_width_synthetic_classification
Title: Effect of Hidden Layer Width on a Small MLP for Synthetic 2D Classification
Short Hypothesis: On a simple synthetic 2D binary classification task (two interleaving half-moons), a one-hidden-layer MLP reaches high test accuracy with only a moderate hidden width; very small widths underfit the nonlinear boundary while very large widths give diminishing or slightly worse returns due to mild overfitting on noisy data. The task is deliberately easy so a correct, runnable baseline is straightforward to obtain.
Related Work: Multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) are the canonical baseline for low-dimensional and tabular classification, and the trade-off between model capacity (width/depth) and generalization is classical. This experiment revisits the width-accuracy relationship on a controlled synthetic dataset (two interleaving half-moons with additive Gaussian noise), where the decision boundary is nonlinear but low-dimensional, making a small MLP an appropriate and reliable model. Unlike compositional-generalization studies that require custom regularizers and sequence models, this task is intentionally simple so that a correct baseline is easy to implement, isolating the study of capacity from implementation difficulty.
Abstract: We study how the hidden-layer width of a small multilayer perceptron (MLP) affects generalization on a synthetic two-dimensional binary classification task. Data are generated in code as two interleaving half-moons with additive Gaussian noise using only numpy; no external datasets are downloaded or used. A baseline MLP with a single hidden layer is trained with standard cross-entropy loss and the Adam optimizer, and we report train and test accuracy. We then sweep the hidden width over a small set of values and measure how test accuracy changes, and we compare against a linear (no-hidden-layer) baseline to confirm the hidden layer is necessary for the nonlinear boundary. The task is deliberately tractable so that a working baseline is easy to implement and runs within seconds, providing valid metrics quickly. The expected finding is that a very small width underfits while moderate widths reach near-perfect accuracy, with diminishing returns at large widths. This provides a clean, low-risk testbed for validating an automated experimentation pipeline end to end.
Experiments: All experiments must be fully self-contained and use only synthetically generated data (no dataset downloads and no internet access). Use numpy to generate the data and PyTorch for the model. 1) Baseline: generate a two-moons dataset in code (e.g., 1000 train and 500 test points with Gaussian noise std 0.2) using numpy; implement a one-hidden-layer MLP (input 2 -> hidden H=16 with ReLU -> output 2), train with Adam (lr=1e-2) and cross-entropy for a fixed number of epochs (e.g., 200 with full-batch or small mini-batches), and report final train and test accuracy as the primary metric. 2) Width sweep: repeat the baseline for hidden width H in {2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64}, recording test accuracy versus width, and plot the curve. 3) Noise robustness: repeat the width sweep at two noise levels (0.1 and 0.3) and report how the width-accuracy curve shifts. 4) Ablation: compare the MLP against a linear model (logistic regression, i.e., no hidden layer) to confirm the hidden layer is necessary for the nonlinear decision boundary. Keep every run small (a few seconds each), deterministic where possible (fix random seeds), and report accuracy as the main metric with simple plots.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The task is intentionally simple and may be too easy to yield novel scientific insight; this is acceptable because the goal is to validate that the automated experimentation pipeline can produce a working implementation and advance through multiple stages on a tractable problem. Test accuracy may saturate near 100% for moderate widths, compressing the dynamic range of the width-accuracy curve. Synthetic half-moons data do not reflect real-world complexity. Compute is negligible, so it is not a limiting factor; the main requirement is that the implementation runs correctly using only in-code synthetic data with no network access.
